facts.text: A furoshiki is a traditional Japanese wrapping cloth that can be used again and again.
The custom of wrapping valuable objects in cloth is said to have begun in the Nara period (710 to 794).
Wrapping cloths came into wide use among ordinary people in the Edo period (1603 to 1867).
In Japanese, furo means bath and shiki means to spread; the name dates from the Edo period.
At communal bathhouses in the Edo period, people wrapped their clothes and belongings in cloth so they would not get mixed up with those of other bathers.
Edo-period travelers carried their things in furoshiki on trips, and many ukiyo-e woodblock prints show travelers with large bundles on their backs.
Over time, all wrapping cloths of this kind came to be called furoshiki.
In 2006 Environment Minister Yuriko Koike created the Mottainai Furoshiki to encourage people to use cloth instead of shopping and paper bags.
The Mottainai Furoshiki was made from fabric made of recycled plastic bottles and carried a bird-and-flower design by the Edo-period artist Ito Jakuchu.
The Japanese word mottainai roughly means what a waste.
